newsitem.title: USA: Case sees strong demand for equipment.
newsitem.headline: Case sees strong demand for equipment.

text.p: Case Inc, which makes and distributes agricultural and construction equipment, said Thursday that its markets continue to be bolstered by solid economic fundamentals.

Worldwide demand for grains and other agricultural products remains exceptionally strong and is growing, Case said in a statement. Commodity prices are favorable and are generally positive for agricultural equipment sales, it said.
In Europe, the demand for lower horsepower tractors has slowed. But Case continues to believe that farm consolidation in Europe will drive greater sales of higher horsepower units.
The construction equipment market is benefiting from historically strong housing starts in North America.
In Europe, housing construction in the U.K. has been brisk, while France and Germany's construction sectors continue to experience significant weakness, Case said.
In the Asia Pacific region, the expected recovery of the Australian housing market has been further delayed due to general economic conditions.
And, in Latin America, economic conditions in Brazil and Mexico have improved and retail sales of agricultural and construction equipment are expected to be strong year-over-year, the company said.

Consistent with 1996, Case said it expects that 1997 unit production and wholesale sales will be at or below retail demand as part of the company's continuing supply chain management plan to further reduce field inventories.

Earlier today, Case reported its 1997 first quarter earnings rose to $62 million from $51 million in the same period a year ago. Revenues increased to $1.23 billion from $1.17 billion in the 1996 first quarter.
The improvement was led by substantial year-over-year gains in the company's Latin American and Asia Pacific regions, Case said.
North America and Europe also reported net sales increases for the quarter, with gains coming primarily from 1996 acquisitions.

"Our growth was fueled by contributions from our 1996 acquisitions and ongoing increases in our Latin American and Asia Pacific regions," said Jean-Pierre Rosso, chairman, president and chief executive officer, in a statement.

Operating earnings for the first quarter were $103 million, down from $126 million for the same period last year. This decline was due to one-time costs associated with the launch and production start-up of the company's MX series tractor, and lower production in preparation for the closure of a Neuss, Germany plant.

During the quarter, the company shifted production of its high volume, mid-horsepower tractor line. This will facilitate the closure of the Neuss plant, which Case identified as the single largest step in the company's long-term restructuring program. The closure will begin to benefit earnings in the second half of 1997, Case said.
Shares of Case were trading off 7/8 to 53-7/8.
